a6tlih0ic6creck71dmn5qb61l.value: Credits: plane projective geometric algebra, with lines as vectors, points as bivectors, the meet as the outer product and the join through the dual, is Charles Gunn's (Geometry, Kinematics, and Rigid Body Mechanics in Cayley-Klein Geometries, 2011) as taught by Gunn and Steven De Keninck (Geometric Algebra for Computer Graphics, SIGGRAPH 2019; bivector.net), and our point convention is ganja.js's (prior art). The interactive construction with dependent shapes that follow a dragged point is what dynamic geometry programs such as Cabri Géomètre (Laborde, 1988) and GeoGebra (Hohenwarter, 2001) do (prior art). That a triangle's angle bisectors meet in one point, the centre of the circle touching its three sides, is a classical theorem (Euclid, Elements IV.4), as are the collapsing compass of Euclid's Elements (I.1 to I.3) and two circles' radical line (Gaultier, 1813; prior art). Keeping plane PGA and carrying a circle as centre and radius, not moving to conformal geometric algebra where circles are blades (Hestenes; Dorst, Fontijne and Mann), is our choice. The tools, the construction and the page are ours.

9o2bd8eqn5t37d08h36hoopqpq.value: Points and lines here are multivectors of Cl(2, 0, 1): a line is a vector, a point a bivector. The line through two points, where two lines cross, the perpendicular from a point and the rest are all products in the one algebra, so nothing special happens when two lines are parallel: they meet at a point at infinity. With the circle tool, a compass, it is a full straightedge-and-compass board.

6q8ckdlhh1e1lva07tsgq6e4hf.value: Where two lines a e₁ + b e₂ + c e₀ cross is their outer product l ∧ m = ½(lm − ml). The line through two points is the same thing seen through the dual, which swaps points and lines: p ∨ q = (p* ∧ q*)*. The perpendicular to l through P is the inner product l · P = ½(lP − Pl), and the parallel is the perpendicular to that. A point reflected in a line is l P l⁻¹ (clifford reflect), and turning about a point C is the sandwich with e^(−θ/2 · C) (clifford exp), because a point with weight 1 squares to −1.

cc8g8t2vbpo9cqu3b0f6olpnfh.value: Circles are not multivectors of this algebra: in plane PGA a vector is a line, and only the conformal algebra Cl(3, 1) makes circles vectors too, at twice the parts per multivector and without the vec3(x, y, 1) picture below. So a circle here is its centre, a point of the algebra, and its radius. A line cuts it half a chord, √(r² − d²), each way from the foot of the perpendicular from the centre (l ∧ (l · C)), moving along the line's own point at infinity, l ∧ e₀. Two circles cross where their radical line, a line you get by subtracting their equations, cuts either of them.

rjsc4ghi1as8qhcjcm2be5j81c.value: These are the same sums a shader does with vec3(x, y, 1): a point's three parts e₂₀, e₀₁, e₁₂ are x, y, 1, and a line's are a, b, c. What the algebra adds is that one product does every construction, in any dimension.
